strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem through a compact instruction-tuning regularizer that combines model-derived confidence with token-level Mixup, without requiring additional annotations. The overall pipeline is understandable.

Tables 1–2 report consistent numerical improvements over NTP across two model families and three training datasets. MT-Bench gains are approximately 0.20–0.29 points, while medical macro-average accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points. The medical evaluations usefully complement the LLM-judged conversational benchmarks.

The ablations provide useful evidence for retaining the NTP objective, using moderate regularization, and obtaining confidence rankings from a smaller reference model. Reporting training hyperparameters and repeated-evaluation standard errors helps readers assess the results.
weaknesses: The decisive gap is the absence of a random-pairing Mixup baseline on the same training data. Section 5.4 changes both the responses and the pairing criterion, so its negative result cannot establish that training dynamics are crucial. Comparing confidence-based pairing against random pairing and single-checkpoint confidence would isolate the defining contribution. This unresolved attribution issue is the main reason for a borderline Findings assessment.

The proposed mechanism remains insufficiently supported. Figure 2’s t-SNE visualization does not demonstrate overfitting among confident examples or improved generalization among unconfident examples. Equation 4 interpolates output logits; general arguments about Mixup do not establish the claimed semantic smoothing and supervision transfer in this setting. Subset-specific training and held-out measurements, or more cautious mechanistic claims, are needed.

The reported repetitions are described as evaluation rounds; independent training runs are not reported. Consequently, the standard errors do not establish robustness to training randomness. Some improvements are also small relative to evaluation uncertainty: Llama/UltraChat’s raw AlpacaEval win rate changes from 5.07 ± 0.12 to 5.11 ± 0.16. The repeated claims of significant improvement need qualification and appropriate paired uncertainty estimates.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the listed optimizer settings. Checkpoint timing, pairing/resampling procedures, sequence-length limits, decoding configurations, and the hyperparameter sweep’s selection criterion are unspecified, and no implementation link is provided. Equation 2 also defines average negative log-likelihood rather than perplexity; this distinction matters because averaging these quantities across checkpoints can produce different confidence rankings.

The cost and scalability motivation is not quantitatively evaluated. SFTMix requires reference-model training and scoring across checkpoints, but no total runtime, memory, or compute-matched comparison is reported. The smaller-reference experiment is encouraging, while experiments on 52K–263K datasets do not establish scalability to datasets of any size.

The broader contribution needs clearer positioning against Park and Caragea (2022), which already combines data cartography and Mixup, and against instruction-tuning regularizers such as NEFTune. These comparisons would clarify the technical advance and practical advantage; their absence particularly limits the main-conference case.
